bib.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions

legacy_report:
SOURCE: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions, Scott M. Lundberg and Su-In Lee, NIPS 2017 (arXiv:1705.07874v2, 25 Nov 2017)

COVERAGE: 31,941 of 31,941 chars, all 10 pages, references included. Pages 6-9 were also rendered and viewed to check flattened maths and read figures. The Supplementary Material (proofs, Max SHAP algorithm, Supp. Figure 1) is not in this PDF.

CLAIMS
- claim: Only one explanation model in the additive class satisfies local accuracy, missingness and consistency: the Shapley values. It is unique for a given input mapping.
  number: 3 properties
  setup: Theoretical. Holds for a fixed simplified-input mapping h_x, so a different mapping gives a different "unique" answer.
  quote: "Under Properties 1-3, for a given simpliﬁed input mappinghx, Theorem 1 shows that there is only one possible additive feature attribution method."
  where: p4
- claim: Methods not based on Shapley values break local accuracy and/or consistency.
  number: none
  setup: Follows from Theorem 1; the Section 2 methods already respect missingness.
  quote: "This result implies that methods not based on Shapley values violate local accuracy and/or consistency (methods in Section 2 already respect missingness)."
  where: p4
- claim: Six existing methods share one explanation model: LIME, DeepLIFT, layer-wise relevance propagation, Shapley regression values, Shapley sampling values, Quantitative Input Influence.
  number: 6
  setup: Definition 1, a linear function of binary simplified inputs.
  quote: "The new class uniﬁes six existing methods, notable because several recent methods in the class lack the proposed desirable properties."
  where: p1
- claim: SHAP values are Shapley values of a conditional expectation of the model, so the definition has a fourth ingredient beyond the three properties.
  number: 3 properties
  setup: Definition; f(z_S) is approximated by E[f(z)|z_S] because most models cannot take arbitrary missing patterns.
  quote: "SHAP values provide the unique additive feature importance measure that adheres to Properties 1-3 and uses conditional expectations to deﬁne simpliﬁed inputs."
  where: p5
- claim: Feature independence and model linearity are optional simplifying assumptions in the estimators, not part of the definition.
  number: none
  setup: Eq. 9-12. Exact computation is called challenging, so the methods approximate.
  quote: "When using these methods, feature independence and model linearity are two optional assumptions simplifying the computation of the expected values"
  where: p5
- claim: Kernel SHAP's regression route uses LIME's mapping, equivalent to Eq. 12, which assumes model linearity as well as independence.
  number: none
  setup: Model-agnostic Kernel SHAP.
  quote: "Since LIME uses a simpliﬁed input mapping that is equivalent to the approximation of the SHAP mapping given in Equation 12, this enables regression-based, model-agnostic estimation of SHAP values."
  where: p6
- claim: Kernel regression is exponential in features; the paper calls it efficient only for small M.
  number: O(2^M + M^3) (the extraction loses the superscripts; checked on the rendered page)
  setup: Linear regression using Theorem 2, under the Eq. 11 or 12 approximation.
  quote: "Since linear regression using Theorem 2 has complexityO(2M +M3), it is efﬁcient for small values ofM if we choose an approximation of the conditional expectations (Equation 11 or 12)."
  where: p6
- claim: LIME's kernel, loss and regulariser are heuristic and do not recover Shapley values.
  number: none
  setup: Default LIME choices in Eq. 2. Theorem 2 gives the choices that do recover them.
  quote: "The LIME choices for these parameters are made heuristically; using these choices, Equation 2 does not recover the Shapley values."
  where: p5
- claim: Faster model-specific approximations exist; Max SHAP is one.
  number: O(M^2) against O(M 2^M) (superscripts checked on the rendered page)
  setup: A max function with M inputs.
  quote: "lets us compute the Shapley values of a max function with M inputs in O(M2) time instead of O(M2M)."
  where: p7
- claim: Linear SHAP reads values from coefficients.
  number: none
  setup: Linear model, assuming input feature independence. Already noted by Štrumbelj and Kononenko.
  quote: "φi(f,x ) =wj(xj−E[xj])"
  where: p6
- claim: Mechanical Turk participants' most common explanation agreed much more with SHAP than with other methods.
  number: 30 and 52 people
  setup: Two toy settings: a sickness score (A) and a three-man max allocation (B). Each human value is the modal answer. Assumes humans who understand the model are the right yardstick. No significance test or response distribution appears.
  quote: "Human feature impact estimates are shown as the most common explanation given among 30 (A) and 52 (B) random individuals, respectively."
  where: p9, Fig 4; "much stronger agreement" on p8
- claim: Kernel SHAP gave more accurate estimates in fewer model evaluations than Shapley sampling, and LIME's values differed from SHAP's.
  number: 200 replicates; 10 features, and 3 of 100 used
  setup: Two decision trees, one feature, a single input, 10th-90th percentile bands. The SHAP estimator used a debiased lasso. The accuracy claim is made "particularly when regularization is added", and the paper gives no numeric error.
  quote: "The 10th and 90th percentiles are shown for 200 replicate estimates at each sample size. (A) A decision tree model using all 10 input features is explained for a single input. (B) A decision tree using only 3 of 100 input features is explained for a single input."
  where: p8, Fig 3
- claim: On MNIST, estimates closer to SHAP gave a larger log-odds change when masking pixels to turn 8 into 3.
  number: 20 random images, 20% of pixels masked, 50k samples
  setup: Pre-trained CNN with 2 convolution and 2 dense layers. DeepLIFT explains a normalised linear layer while SHAP and LIME explain the output, so the targets differ. LIME was modified to single-pixel segmentation.
  quote: "SHAP and LIME were both run with 50k samples (Supplementary Figure 1); to improve performance, LIME was modiﬁed to use single pixel segmentation over the digit pixels. To match [7], we masked 20% of the pixels chosen to switch the predicted class from 8 to 3"
  where: p9

LIMITS
- There is no tree-specific method here. TreeExplainer comes from the later paper the note cites.
- Empirical support is small: two toy user studies, two synthetic-scale decision trees on one input, one MNIST class pair on 20 images. No real-world dataset or decision-maker study.
- The user study measures agreement with modal human answers, not whether explanations help anyone. Its yardstick is stated as an assumption (p8).
- DeepLIFT appears only in Fig 4B, not 4A, although the text says all three methods were compared in two settings.
- Correlated features are not studied. Fig 1's caption only says order matters when the model is non-linear or features are dependent. Causality is not discussed.
- The authors name as next steps "faster model-type-speciﬁc estimation methods that make fewer assumptions" and interaction effects (p9).

BUILDS ON: Shapley 1953 (value); Young 1985 (uniqueness axioms); Charnes et al. 1988 (equivalent quadratic formulation, found during preparation); Lipovetsky and Conklin 2001 (Shapley regression); Štrumbelj and Kononenko 2014 (sampling); Bach et al. 2015 (LRP); Ribeiro et al. 2016 (LIME); Datta, Sen and Zick 2016 (QII); Shrikumar et al. 2016 and 2017 (DeepLIFT).

CODE: none in the paper. It links https://github.com/slundberg/shap (p1, footnote 1).

FIGURES (read off the images, approximate, so not listed as quoted claims)
- Fig 4, p9, human/SHAP/LIME/DeepLIFT bars: the best candidate, since one glance shows the disagreement. In A, Human and SHAP are about 1.0 for fever and cough while LIME is about -1.15. In B, Human and SHAP are 3, 2, 0, LIME about 2, 1, 0, Orig. DeepLIFT 5, 0, 0.
- Fig 2A, p7, Shapley kernel vs LIME kernels over 2^15 subsets: shows weight concentrating on very small and very large subsets.
- Fig 1, p5, base value to f(x) by conditioning: explains baseline and additivity faster than prose, and notes that order matters. Not viewed; caption only.
- Fig 3, p8, estimates vs model evaluations: shows LIME converging to a different value (about 0.13 against about 0.33 in the dense panel).
- Fig 5, p9, MNIST masking: median log-odds change about 32, 42, 47, 41 (Orig. DeepLIFT, New DeepLIFT, SHAP, LIME). LIME and New DeepLIFT overlap SHAP's range, so it is weaker evidence.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction flattens maths. Examples are "O(2M +M3)", "215 vectors" (2^15), "O(M2M)" and the Shapley kernel fraction. Do not copy formulas from the text layer; use the rendered pages (p6, p7).
- Paper typos, as printed on the rendered pages: "Kernal SHAP" (p8), "menthod" (p3). Corollary 1 mixes indices (φ_i with w_j, x_j).
- No embedded instructions.
- The temporary PNGs are in /var/folders/f9/kl6j_lwx5p73h75kz13k6www0000gn/T/tmp.GzqAMVWsJy. No repo files were changed.

Correct: the six methods (3 + 3 Shapley-based); the three properties; 30 and 52 people; two small problems; NIPS 2017; Kernel SHAP's independence assumption.

Mismatches:
1. Line 211, "Other model types use the slower Kernel SHAP." This conflicts with the paper's Section 4.2, which gives Linear, Low-Order, Max and Deep SHAP as faster options. Kernel SHAP is the model-agnostic option, and Shapley sampling is another. "Slower" is not sourced here, and the sentence carries no citation.
2. Line 209, "than LIME and DeepLIFT did." DeepLIFT is plotted only in the second problem (Fig 4B). LIME is in both. The paper's prose does say all three were compared, so this is a mismatch with the figure rather than the sentence.
3. Line 209, local accuracy as "the numbers sum to the prediction." The paper's Eq. 5 includes the base φ0. This also sits awkwardly with the note's own line 325 ("sum to the prediction minus the baseline") and the line 255 output, where 2.559 alone is not 0.172.

Under-qualified:
4. Line 209, "the unique solution." It omits "for a given simplified input mapping". Uniqueness does not choose the mapping or background, and line 296 only partly covers this as a pitfall.
5. Line 326, "What three properties define SHAP?" The paper's definition adds conditional expectations for simplified inputs (p5).
6. Line 267, Kernel SHAP "assumes feature independence." This is true but incomplete: the regression route ties to Eq. 12, which also assumes model linearity (p5-6). The paper also calls these assumptions optional simplifications, so they belong to the estimator and not to SHAP itself.
7. Line 209, missingness as "an absent feature gets zero." In the paper this means x'_i = 0 in the simplified input, meaning not present. A learner could read it as value zero, yet the same note shows `capital-gain 0` at -0.253 (deck line ~419 too). Worth a clause.
8. Line 209, consistency gloss. The paper compares two models and requires the contribution not to fall for all inputs z' ("regardless of the other inputs"). The note's "matters more to the model" drops both conditions.
9. Line 328, "SHAP's weights come from the Shapley axioms." That applies to Kernel SHAP's regression kernel (Theorem 2), not to SHAP generally.

Missing setup:
10. Line 209, the human study. Missing: the human value is the modal answer, the agreement yardstick is an assumption the authors state, and no significance test is reported. "With 30 and 52 people" reads as more evidence than that.
11. Missing from the note entirely, available if wanted: Kernel SHAP's O(2^M + M^3) and the paper's "efficient for small values of M". That would give line 211's cost claim a sourced setup.

Not from this source: line 267's correlated-features sentence and all causal claims. The paper supports only Fig 1's order-dependence remark and says nothing on causality. The note does not attribute them to it, so this is not a mismatch, but they need their own support.
